# A model nobody can audit is a recommendation taken on trust {.unnumbered}

The Climate Policy Assessment Tool (CPAT), built by the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund, estimates what carbon pricing and related policies do to energy use, emissions, revenue, growth and households for more than 180 countries. Ministries use its numbers to set rates and sequence reforms. Until recently almost nobody could check them: the legacy model was a very large Excel workbook, and its 57,000-word mitigation documentation disagreed with the model in places.

The papers in this section make the model legible and check it; section 6 extends it. They are written so that an economist can understand each piece in an afternoon, and each points to the code and documentation in the CPAT-AI repository for the detail.

# What the model computes (paper 5.1) {.unnumbered}

The mitigation module is six blocks and about eighteen equations. Retail prices are built up from supply cost, existing taxes, subsidies and the new carbon charge. Fuel use responds through income, usage and efficiency elasticities. An engineering power model dispatches, retires and invests. Emissions and revenue follow by accounting identities, and revenue moves GDP a year later through fiscal multipliers. In the paper's stylized example a \$50 per tonne carbon price cuts industrial coal use by about a third and road fuel use by about 6 percent. The power model also reports investment spending, priced at default costs of capital of 7.5, 10, 12.5 and 15 percent for high-, upper-middle-, lower-middle- and low-income countries. Road transport is the module's weak joint: CPAT describes it three times, in a simple fuel equation, an engineering fleet model and a co-benefits module, and the three are not consistent: the co-benefits module always takes vehicle-km from the fleet model, even when fuel use and emissions follow the fuel equation, so the change in driving it values need not match the modelled change in fuel use (papers 5.1, 5.3 and 6.4 flag this; CPAT-AI register issue I100). The paper gives the corrected equation wherever the documentation is wrong and proposes a penalty-based investment rule as an alternative to the logit share rule, which never lets a technology's share reach zero.

# Rebuild it twice (paper 5.2) {.unnumbered}

The model was rebuilt twice in October 2026 with AI coding agents, Claude Code and GitHub Copilot, doing most of the construction: once as a readable Excel workbook generated by code (Excel-AI) and once as a Python model (Coded CPAT) that reproduces it number for number. One rule governed both: errors in the legacy model are fixed and never copied; questionable but intended choices are copied and logged. The rebuild found 228 bugs in the legacy model, 24 of them high priority because they change standard results, together with 135 issues (intended choices open to question), 35 deliberate departures and 20 errors in the documentation. Writing the model a second time found seven more bugs in the first rebuild. The lesson is general: specify a policy model by shared variable codes, build it at least twice and test it at every change.

# Check it against data and other models (papers 5.3 and 5.4) {.unnumbered}

The published validation shows a model good for ranges and policy comparisons, not point forecasts. CPAT reproduces its base year by construction, follows the trend of emissions in back-casts from 2000 for several countries, and gives baselines and carbon-price responses of the same order as other energy models; it fits poorly where prices are hard to forecast, as for China. The rebuilt versions reproduce the legacy blocks to many decimal places. Every published check predates the bug fixes and should be rerun.

The price elasticities matter more than any other input, and most of them pass. Seven of ten fuel-sector defaults lie within the range of published meta-analyses; three are too high, and road gasoline is double the estimate corrected for publication bias. Two structural choices matter more than any single value: the full long-run response is applied within one year, and there are no cross-price terms. Paper 5.4 sets out a protocol for future updates.

# Extend it where policy needs it (section 6) {.unnumbered}

Extensions belong outside the core, so that the core stays small enough to audit. Section 6 adds five modular upgrades, each of which reads CPAT's prices, fuel use and emissions and adds one piece of economics: the Total Effective Carbon Price, which measures any policy mix as one carbon tax (paper 6.1); the CBAM Policy Tool, which measures exporters' exposure to the EU carbon border adjustment (paper 6.2); a public investment extension that prices the clean capital and tests whether the budget should pay for it (paper 6.3); a common activity layer that links CPAT to SISEPUEDE, the CBAM tool and the Future Technology Transformations models (paper 6.4); and the Macro-Fiscal-Energy Scenario Tool, which carries a climate program through to growth, revenue and debt (paper 6.5).
